references.text: Jesus 'had to' travel through Samaria on his way. In [ref:Luk 9:51-53|Luke 9:51-53], Jesus travels through Samaria on the way to Jerusalem, and the Samaritans reject him – which shows the Jewish-Samaritan tension underlying John 4.
In [ref:Luk 17:11|Luke 17:11], Jesus travels along the border between Samaria and Galilee, another text showing that Samaria lay on the route between Judea and Galilee.

The result of Jesus 'having to' travel through Samaria is described in [ref:Joh 4:39-42|John 4:39-42], where many Samaritans come to faith. The divine 'had to' (ἔδει) points to God's plan of salvation that also includes the Samaritans.
The Greek word ἔdei ('it was necessary') is also used in [ref:Joh 3:14|John 3:14] about how the Son of Man 'must' be lifted up. In both places, the word points to a divine necessity in Jesus' work.
[ref:Joh 4:9|John 4:9] explains the background for why it was remarkable that Jesus 'had to' travel through Samaria: Jews had no dealings with Samaritans.

In [ref:Apg 1:8|Acts 1:8], Jesus commands his disciples to be his witnesses 'in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.' That Jesus himself visited Samaria laid the foundation for the spread of the gospel there, cf. [ref:Apg 8:5-8|Acts 8:5-8].
In [ref:Apg 8:5-8|Acts 8:5-8], Philip preaches the gospel in Samaria with great response. This is the fulfillment of what began with Jesus' visit to Samaria in John 4.

[ref:2 Kong 17:24|2 Kings 17:24] describes the historical background for the Samaritans: The king of Assyria settled foreign peoples in the cities of Samaria after the fall of the northern kingdom, which led to the mixed population that the Jews later rejected.
